What still needs to be done
It's January 2030. Friedrich Mertens is coming from Lübeck to Berlin next Saturday, with his granddaughter. Mrs Hoffmann now knows everything. Mara and Lena are making a list of the preparations.
So, what still needs to be done? We've only got five days left.
First the piano has to be tuned. It hasn't been tuned for two years. Mrs Hoffmann says it sounds like an old tram.
The piano tuner has already been booked. He's coming on Thursday. What else?
Friedrich has to be picked up from the main station. He's ninety-five and uses a wheelchair. A taxi with a ramp has to be booked.
Andrei's doing that. And how does he get up to the fourth floor? There's no lift.
That's the biggest problem. He can't be carried up the stairs, it's too dangerous. And Mrs Hoffmann can't be carried down any more. She's too weak.
Hm. And what if they don't meet in the flat, but in the courtyard? At the window?
In January? At minus five degrees? No. But wait… Ludwig's flat is on the first floor. There are only twelve steps up to it. And Ludwig has room.
And the piano? The grand piano can't be brought down to the first floor!
No. But Mrs Hoffmann has an old piano in the cellar that she never uses. Piotr says it can be carried up in an hour. It just has to be tuned.
An old piano in the cellar. Like in the war. Mara, it's perfect.

The conjugated modal is in position 2; at the end come the participle and “werden” (the passive infinitive):
Formula: modal + … + participle + werden. “Was muss noch gemacht werden?” = What still needs to be done?
In a subordinate clause, the modal goes last: “…, dass der Flügel gestimmt werden muss.”
The passive in the Perfekt is formed with “sein” + participle + “worden” (the special form, without ge-!):
“worden” only in the passive! “Er ist Lehrer geworden” (he became a teacher) vs. “Er ist abgeholt worden” (he was picked up).
In speech, the Präteritum (“wurde gelesen”) and the Perfekt (“ist gelesen worden”) mean the same thing. The Perfekt is slightly more common in conversation.

The parcel from Lübeck had been brought up to the fourth floor by Mara on 30 December. Mrs Hoffmann had looked at it for a long time, without opening it. She had read the sender three times, with her glasses and without. Then she had asked, in a voice Mara had never heard before: “What have you done, child?”

Mara had told her everything. About Andrei, who had searched for three weeks. About the short news item on the internet. About the copy of the letter, which had been sent on 23 December. Mrs Hoffmann had listened with her eyes closed. Then she had opened the brown paper, very slowly, as if it might break.

Inside was a violin bow. Old, made of dark wood, with white horsehair. Something was engraved on the handle, very small: “G. 1961”. And underneath there was a letter, short, in large, shaky handwriting: “Dear Grete. I bought this bow for you in August 1961. I wanted to give it to you on Monday, so that you'd hand it back to me every time we played together. There was never another Monday. I've kept it for sixty-five years. I never stopped hoping. If you'll allow me, I'll come and fetch it. Your Friedrich.”

Mrs Hoffmann had held the bow in her hands for a whole hour. She hadn't cried. She had only said: “He always said I held the bow too tightly. Like a knife. He showed me a hundred times how to hold it loosely.” Then she had looked at Mara and said: “Write and tell him to come. Quickly. Neither of us has much time left.”

And now it was Saturday, 18 January, and everything had been prepared. The old piano had been carried by Piotr, Andrei and Jakob from the cellar into Ludwig's flat, which had taken two hours and three beer breaks. The tuner had come on Thursday and said this piano hadn't been tuned since the war. “It sounds as if it had been asleep for seventy years,” he had said. Now it sounded like new. Well, almost.

That morning Mrs Hoffmann had been carried down the three floors on her chair by Andrei and Jakob. She was now sitting in Ludwig's armchair, under the yellow lamp, in her navy blue dress, with freshly done hair. Lena had done it for her that morning. In her lap lay the bow. Ludwig sat next to her. He didn't say anything. He just held her hand.

At three a taxi stopped in front of the house. Andrei had booked it, a big taxi with a ramp. First a young woman with short blonde hair got out of the taxi: Sophie, Friedrich's granddaughter, who had accompanied him from Lübeck. Then a wheelchair was slowly lowered down the ramp. In it sat a very old, thin man in a grey coat, with a black violin case on his knees. He looked up at the windows of the old house, one after another, as if he were looking for something.

The twelve steps up to the first floor were climbed with four men: Andrei, Jakob, Piotr and Thomas, who had come specially from Munich. Fritz ran ahead excitedly, Bruno behind. Mara opened the door. Then she stepped aside.

Friedrich was pushed into the living room. Mrs Hoffmann was sitting in the armchair. They looked at each other. Sixty-five years. A lifetime. A wall that had been built and that had fallen. Two old people with white hair and trembling hands, looking at each other like two young musicians on a platform in August.
You're late, Friedrich. You said: see you Monday.

Friedrich laughed. A quiet, fragile laugh that turned into a cough, and then into something else that was no longer laughter. Sophie put her hand on his shoulder. Mrs Hoffmann held out her hand, and Friedrich took it, and they stayed like that for a long time, without a word, while everyone else in the room pretended to be looking out of the window.

Then Mrs Hoffmann said: “I have your bow. Have you got the violin?” Friedrich nodded. Sophie opened the violin case. The violin was taken out carefully and tuned, by trembling fingers that still knew exactly what they were doing. Mrs Hoffmann was led to the piano by Ludwig and Mara. She gave Friedrich the bow. “This time I'm giving it back to you,” she said. “As I promised.”

They played the Brahms sonata. Not perfectly. Slowly, with pauses, with wrong notes, with a piano that had slept for seventy years and a violin played by a ninety-five-year-old man. But for the first time since 1961, the sonata no longer sounded as if half of it were missing. Everyone in the room was crying. Even Ludwig, who this time didn't say it was the dust. Even Fritz, who had lain down under the piano and was howling softly along with them.

When the last note had died away, Friedrich lowered the violin. He looked at Grete. “You still hold the bow too tightly,” he said. “I've told you that a hundred times.” Mrs Hoffmann smiled, looking younger than Mara had ever seen her. “Then you'll have to show me once more,” she said. “We have time, after all.”

Later, after Lena had brought coffee and cake and everyone was sitting round the big table, Sophie told the story quietly, while her grandfather and Grete were whispering to each other at the piano. Friedrich had waited two years after the Wall was built. Then he had gone to Vienna, where he had been offered a position in an orchestra. Later he had married a cellist from Hamburg, Sophie's grandmother, who had died ten years ago. It had been a good marriage, Sophie said, an honest one. “But every year, on 13 August,” she said, “Grandpa played the Brahms sonata alone in his room. Only the violin part. Grandma knew. She never asked. She just closed the door every time, so that he wouldn't be disturbed.” Mara looked at the two old people at the piano. She thought that some loves don't end, they just wait. Sixty-five years, if they have to.

Friedrich stayed in Berlin for a week, in a small hotel on Kollwitzplatz that Andrei had booked for him. Every afternoon Sophie brought him to Kastanienallee, and every afternoon the two of them played in Ludwig's living room, for an hour, sometimes two. On the last day, Friedrich said to Mara: “I'll come again in the spring. And then we'll take Grete to Lübeck, to the Baltic Sea. She hasn't seen the sea for forty years.”
